gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the 2 kWh picks can't be compared on their headline specs. Anker's '10,000 cycles' for the SOLIX S2000 is to 60% capacity (6,000 to 80%), its '3,000 W' is peak against a 1,500 W rated output, and only the BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 has an independently measured AC discharge. Two reviewers measured 1,910 Wh and about 1,990 Wh, enough for two 700 Wh charges at the 880–935 Wh each that one charge takes.
standout_why: I compared against PowerStationGearLab (cited, 2026-11-05), PowerBencher (rank 2) and our own 2026-11-03 page. GearLab gives the cycle-life basis for some units (Anker C1000 Gen 2 at 80%, Jackery 1000 Plus at 70%, RIVER 2 Pro at 80%). It states no measured usable AC energy for any unit, gives no cycle basis for the DELTA 3 Max and doesn't cover the S2000. PowerBencher gives the basis for the RIVER 2 Pro and DELTA 2 Max only, measures nothing, and doesn't separate X-Boost from surge. Our page has StorageReview's 1,910 Wh but not APH's 2-hour drain test, no cycle-life basis and nothing on the S2000. ChatGPT's plain chat made the S2000 its top pick with no AC rating and no cycle footnote.
decides: It confirms the Elite 200 V2. It is the only ~2 kWh candidate with measured AC delivery, 1,910–1,990 Wh, and that covers two 700 Wh charges at 1,760–1,870 Wh with 40–230 Wh to spare. ChatGPT's S2000 pick is unmeasured. At 0.85 of its rated capacity it delivers about 1,709 Wh, which is short of a second full charge. Its 10,000-cycle headline is to 60%, not the 80% the others use. Rated vs peak output doesn't matter for an e-bike charger, which draws 100–300 W, but the table should not set Anker's 3,000 W peak against BLUETTI's 2,600 W continuous.

findings.label: US store price
findings.source_title: BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 Portable Power Station | 2,600W 2,080Wh
findings.note: Read with storecheck.py search on bluettipower.com, then opened the page. The page gives the capacity as both 2,080 Wh (product title) and 2,073.6 Wh (elsewhere). The page states no cycle life, weight or efficiency.

findings.label: Rated vs Power Lifting output
findings.value: 2,600 W continuous; up to 3,900 W only for resistive loads in Power Lifting mode
findings.source_title: BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 Portable Power Station
findings.note: The 3,900 W is a voltage-reduction mode for heaters and kettles, not a surge rating. Don't compare it with other makers' surge or peak figures.

findings.label: Measured AC discharge (StorageReview)
findings.source_title: Portable Power Meets Lab-Grade Reliability: BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 Review
findings.note: Review dated 2025-04-25. StorageReview does not state the load. 1,910 / 2,073.6 = 92.1%.

findings.label: Measured AC drain test (APH Networks, Jonathan Kwan)
findings.value: 2,028 Wh on the station's display at 1,006 W; about 1,990 Wh at the heater (987 W × 2 h 1 min)
findings.note: Review dated 2025-02-21. Load was a constant 987 W heater; the station showed 1,006 W. 2,028 Wh matches 1,006 W × 2.017 h, so it is the station's own output figure. At the heater: 987 × 2.017 = 1,990 Wh, 96% of rated. At the 100–300 W of an e-bike charger, expect nearer StorageReview's 92%.

findings.label: Cycle life basis and weight
findings.value: 6,000+ cycles to 80% of original capacity; 24.2 kg (53.4 lb)
findings.note: Maker spec quoted by APH Networks. The BLUETTI US product page does not state it, and I couldn't extract text from the manual PDF.

findings.label: Cycle life basis
findings.source_title: Anker SOLIX S2000 Portable Power Station
findings.note: From Anker's comparison table. Footnote 5 ties the 15-year lifespan to 'up to 10,000 charge cycles' while 'retaining more than 60%'. On the 80% basis the other makers use, it is 6,000 cycles, the same as the Elite 200 V2.

findings.label: Rated vs peak AC; capacity; weight; price
findings.value: 1,500 W rated / 3,000 W peak; 2,010 Wh; 35.7 lb (16.2 kg); $699.99, 5-year warranty, ships in 2–3 weeks
findings.source_title: Anker SOLIX S2000 Portable Power Station
findings.note: The page also shows $999.99 in an offer block. ChatGPT's card showed $749.99 at Best Buy (2026-11-07), and I didn't check that. 2,010 × 0.85 (Jackery's factor, also within EcoFlow's 0.80–0.90 AC guidance, as cited by GearLab) = 1,709 Wh. That is below the 1,760–1,870 Wh two 700 Wh charges need.

findings.label: Idle draw, AC on: claimed vs measured (ESS News, Andrew Riha)
findings.value: 6 W claimed; about 2 W measured (100% to 99% state of charge over 10 h, no load)
findings.source_title: Anker Solix S2000 review: 2 kWh power station built for the long haul
findings.note: Review dated 2026-05-19. The 6 W claim is on Anker's page (internal test). ESS News reported no Wh delivered on AC discharge.

findings.label: Idle draw, inverter on, no load (The Solar Lab)
findings.source_title: EcoFlow DELTA 3 Max Review: A Step Forward or a Step Sideways?
findings.note: No date or author on the page. Leaving the AC on overnight between two charges (about 10 h) costs about 270 Wh, versus about 20–60 Wh on the S2000. The review has no AC discharge test, and it says EcoFlow dropped X-Boost marketing for this series.

findings.label: Usable-energy factors the makers publish (as cited by the GearLab rival)
findings.value: Jackery ×0.85; EcoFlow 0.80–0.90 for AC; Anker 'typically 10–15%' charging losses; GearLab plans on 70% reaching the bike
findings.source_title: Best Power Station for E-Bike Charging (2026): 5 Picks and the Charges-per-Battery Math
findings.note: The rival page dated 2026-11-05 has these factors but no measured usable Wh for any unit. It gives the DELTA 3 Max as 2,400 W / 4,800 W surge, $879, cycle life not stated.
